title: The reason your AI trading backtest is lying to you has a name: multiple testing. I ran the correction and 0 of my 20 best survived.
author: espressodoppioo
selftext:
If you are testing AI/ML strategies and picking the best one, here is the trap almost nobody accounts for, and it quietly kills most 'my AI bot works' results.

If you test one strategy and it has a Sharpe of 3, that is interesting. If you test 35,000 and your best has a Sharpe of 3, that is roughly what pure noise produces. The maximum of thousands of random trials is large by construction. Your grid search, hyperparameter tuning and feature selection are one giant multiple-testing machine, and the winner it hands you is the luckiest draw as much as the best one.

There is a correction: the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (Bailey and Lopez de Prado). It asks, given how many configs I actually tried, what is the probability this result is real and not just the best of N noise draws.

I ran it on my own sweep. N = 35,562 configurations. My best finalist had an annualized Sharpe of 3.36 and looked bulletproof in isolation. Deflated Sharpe: 0.115. The hurdle was 0.95. Zero of my 20 best cleared it.

That stung, but it is the point: once you account for how hard you searched, none beat luck. Cheaper to learn on a backtest than with money. It also matches the academic finding (McLean and Pontiff) that published predictors lose \~26% of their edge out-of-sample, largely because publishing is itself a selection over many tested ideas.

The kicker: the more compute you throw at the search, the worse this gets, which is the opposite of most people's intuition. Bigger sweep, more inflated winner.



Does anyone here track their trial count and deflate for it, or is it walk-forward and hope? Curious how many people account for the search itself.

comments.author: hakobpapazian
comments.body:
The part most people miss is that even your N is understated. 35,562 is the configs in the sweep, but the real trial count includes every idea you tried and dropped before you got to that sweep, every feature you tested and abandoned, every strategy that never made it to the grid. That's all multiple testing too, it just wasn't logged.

Human in the loop selection is the untracked part. You look at a chart, decide the setup isn't working, tweak it, look again. That's a trial. Nobody counts those, and over months of research it's usually a bigger N than the formal sweep. So the deflated number is still optimistic, which is grim but worth sitting with.

To answer your actual question, most people are doing walk forward and hoping. And walk forward doesn't save you if you ran 200 walk forward variants and kept the one that looked good, that's the same trap wearing a different hat. The only real defense I've found is deciding the mechanism first, why should this edge exist, and only then testing it, so you're not fishing.

comments.author: TigerKR
comments.body: I tested near a trillion (not an exaggeration, was running sims on AWS cloud) different scenarios, out of that, had 500 that passed strict testing — but before noise calibration. After noise calibration, 1 passed. Incredibly deflating. Now I’m also trying to reverse engineer a strategy from my thousands of live winning trades.

comments.author: Flaky-Leadership-749
comments.body:
I have a large solana token dataset - 30m candles historically for quite some time with indicators/signals that get thrown for setups and breakouts - I've found my setups beat my breakouts long term after live trading vs breakouts winning in my historical back testing.

And that's two patterns that I found out of.... Tens of thousands that I've tested...

I'm actually looking for others that do this type of thing - and a community to join if one exists. Any recommendations are welcome. I feel like a hermit. Over here with all this value to share and no toothbrush. Poor gator. 🐊🪥

comments.author: Brilliant-Mulberry55
comments.body:
Man, this is spot on. Kudos to you for actually running Deflated Sharpe—almost nobody accounts for how hard their grid search fished for that top result. And like u/hakobpapazian mentioned, the real number of attempts is way higher once you include all the quick chart tweaks and abandoned ideas along the way.

We run into this all the time, and the only way we stay honest is by treating the *entire parameter sweep* as one single experiment (using White's Reality Check across all runs) rather than looking at the #1 winner alone. We also always nudge the winning parameters slightly up and down to make sure they sit on a wide, stable plateau rather than an overfit spike. It hurts watching 20 "bulletproof" backtests get rejected by the math, but it's way better than letting them blow up a live account.
